newsitem.title: INDIA: Britain's Major starts tour of South Asia.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major starts tour of South Asia.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, facing an election in no more than four months, arrived in Calcutta on Thursday for a week-long tour of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh aimed at boosting British trade in the region.
During his visit, Major was set to meet Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and Pakistan's caretaker premier, Meraj Khalid, as well as opposition leaders.
Major, on his last scheduled foreign trip before the general election, was accompanied by more than 50 top British businessmen.
The prime minister's decision to leave Britain in the midst of a bitter pre-election campaign surprised even senior ministers in his Conservative government.
Major's Conservatives are lagging 20 points behind in the polls, and ruling party members of parliament are growing increasingly nervous about the stubbornness of the opposition Labour Party's lead.
Major said on arrival from London that the potential for growth in business between Britain and India was vast.
The British prime minister said he agreed to the visit when members of the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) asked him last June to be the keynote speaker at their annual meeting in Calcutta.
Major said the visit "could be no clearer demonstration of the confidence of British business in the potential of the Indian economy".

Among the businessmen representing a wide range of sectors including insurance, aerospace and merchant banking were British Airways Plc chief executive Robert Ayling and Iain Vallance, chairman of British Telecommunications Plc.
Major stressed the importance of his visit to India at the start of the country's 50th year of independence from British rule. Queen Elizabeth was due to visit the region later in the year.
The tour was to begin with the signing of some minor trade agreements.
Major was set to visit a British aid project in a Calcutta slum before talks with Deve Gowda and a keynote speech to Indian businessmen at CII's annual conference on Thursday afternoon.
Major was due to leave Calcutta on Friday for the southern city of Bangalore, the capital of Deve Gowda's home state of Karnataka, before continuing to Bangladesh and Pakistan.

British ambassador to India, David Gore-Booth, told reporters on Wednesday that in addition to business, Major and Deve Gowda were expected to discuss regional security, militancy and Commonwealth affairs.
Six joint ventures would be signed between Indian and British businessmen in the insurance and engineering sectors, the Press Trust of India quoted Gore-Booth as saying.
Major, a keen sports fan, was expected to snatch an hour or two in Calcutta on Thursday to watch the Lancashire cricket side take on a local team.
